title: Local Models: Trust, Control, Optimization — Carter Abdallah, NVIDIA

primary.label: Post-Training & Continual Learning
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 55%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The panel discusses open models, trust, and deployment strategy as cross-domain themes without focusing on a single application vertical. The arguments about post-training, efficiency, and local deployment apply broadly across all AI use cases.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: The panel is fundamentally about the tools and platforms used by builders working with open models—the training stack, model weights, datasets, post-training infrastructure, and the developer ecosystem around open model customization.

domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: Enterprise use cases are a significant theme: finance automation (Ramp/Saber), cost predictability for CFOs, token spend management, and the shift from closed APIs to self-hosted open models for enterprise workloads.

summary: A panel moderated by Carter Abdallah (NVIDIA) brings together three layers of the open AI model stack: Vincent Weisser (Prime Intellect, training infrastructure and RL environments), Lucas Atkins (Arcee AI, model pretraining — Trinity 400B MoE), and Chris Alexiuk (NVIDIA Nemotron, optimization and deployment). The discussion centers on trust, control, and optimization of open models. The panel argues trust—distinct from safety—comes from inspectability: open models are directories of files with readable code, while closed API claims are unverifiable by construction. Post-training is framed as the most economically viable customization layer, with Ramp cited as specializing an open model to beat frontier models on finance tasks at a fraction of the cost. The "mismanaged genius" concept argues that a model optimized across every harness is optimal for nobody's; open weights let builders fit models to specific harnesses. Output ownership is presented as a critical differentiator: closed-API terms of service prohibit training on outputs, while open models enable a data flywheel through trace capture and replay. The OpenMDW license (adopted by Trinity and planned for Nemotron) explicitly permits using outputs for training. On optimization, the panel invokes the Linux analogy: hyper-optimization requires broad community contribution under resource constraints. Predictions include open models reaching frontier capability within 12 months, capable local models on phones and MacBooks within the year, agent operating systems replacing traditional OSs, diffusion-based text architectures, and a goal of 10–15% of AI users running models locally—up from a near-zero baseline.
whyItMatters: The panel synthesizes three complementary layers of the open AI stack — training infrastructure (Prime Intellect), model pretraining (Arcee/Trinity), and optimization/deployment (NVIDIA Nemotron) — into a coherent strategic argument that open models are an economically superior architecture for enterprise AI, not merely a philosophical preference. The software engineering concepts (post-training specialization, data flywheel, RL environments, model-harness co-design, OpenMDW licensing) describe the concrete engineering practices that make open models practically viable. The AI concepts (mismanaged genius, trust vs. safety, specialization tradeoff, Jevons paradox, capability trajectory) provide the theoretical and economic framing for why those practices matter. Trust (inspectability), control (post-training specialization), and optimization (community-driven efficiency) are presented as three reinforcing dimensions of the same thesis: open models enable customization, cost predictability, and data ownership that closed APIs structurally cannot provide. The 'mismanaged genius' concept connects engineering practice (harness-specific fine-tuning) to the economic argument for specialization over generalization. The OpenMDW license bridges the legal and data-flywheel dimensions by making output-based training explicitly permissible. The Linux analogy ties the optimization argument to a proven historical precedent. The predictions about local compute, agent OSs, diffusion architectures, and knowledge worker agents connect these near-term practices to a platform-shift thesis for the next 12 months. Together, these concepts form a complete stack-level worldview where every layer — from licensing to infrastructure to model architecture — reinforces the case for open models as the enterprise substrate.
temporalContext: The panel was published on 2026-08-07 and recorded in the context of a rapidly shifting open-model landscape in mid-2026. Arcee's Trinity family moved to OpenMDW-1.1 on 2026-05-29 (approximately 10 weeks before this panel), and NVIDIA announced plans to adopt OpenMDW-1.1 for Nemotron at or around the same time. NVIDIA had recently announced Nemotron 3.5 Lightning in August 2026, shortly before or concurrent with this panel. The panel makes 12-month forward predictions (projecting to approximately August 2027), including open models reaching frontier-level capability, capable models running locally on MacBooks and phones, agent operating systems shipping on computers, and 10–15% of AI users having run a model locally. Web research was conducted as of 2026-08-23, 16 days after video publication, providing near-current verification of the organizational and product claims made during the panel.
takeaways: Prime Intellect, Arcee, and NVIDIA's Nemotron represent complementary layers of the open AI stack: training infrastructure, model pretraining, and optimization for speed and local deployment.
Post-training is the most accessible and economically viable way to customize open models for specific enterprise use cases, enabling specialized models that beat frontier models at lower cost.
A model optimized across every harness is optimal for nobody's—open weights let builders fit models to their specific harness (the 'mismanaged genius' framing).

Closed-API terms of service prohibit training on outputs, while open models let users save traces and build a data flywheel; Nemotron and Trinity adopted the open MDW license to explicitly permit this.
Most people do not need frontier-level intelligence for 90% of tasks; open models let you specialize at the expense of generalization, which is the right tradeoff for most use cases.
Efficiency must happen in the open—like Linux, hyper-optimization requires a broad community of contributors working under resource constraints that closed companies cannot replicate.
Closed and open models will coexist: closed APIs serve as accessible consumer layers (like Macs), while open models form the infrastructure layer (like Linux) running enterprises and clouds.
Open models are expected to reach Fable-level capability within 12 months, enabling a wave of new AI startups and a shift from chatbots to general knowledge worker agents.
Lucas hopes 10–15% of AI users will have run a model locally—up from a near-zero baseline—and calls this the most consequential year for how AI gets distributed.

Chris predicts capable local models on MacBooks within the year, swarms of specialized models, diffusion-based text architectures, and computers shipping with agent operating systems instead of traditional OSs.

concepts.name: Mismanaged genius
concepts.explanation: A model tuned across every harness is optimal for nobody's — we leave important capability on the table by not fitting models into specific harnesses. Open weights let builders post-train models for their specific harness, achieving customization impossible with closed models.
concepts.importance: Core conceptual framing that bridges engineering practice (harness-specific fine-tuning) with the economic argument for open models — specialization at the expense of generalization is the right tradeoff for most use cases, and only open weights enable it.

concepts.name: Trust vs. safety distinction
concepts.explanation: Trust (access and inspectability of model internals) is distinct from safety (output reliability). Conflating the two mischaracterizes open models as untrustworthy. Open models earn trust through inspectability — they are directories of files with readable code.
concepts.importance: Reframes the open vs. closed debate around a precise conceptual distinction that is often blurred in industry discourse, providing a clearer analytical framework for evaluating model deployment decisions.

concepts.name: Specialization vs. generalization tradeoff
concepts.explanation: Most people do not need frontier-level intelligence for 90% of tasks. Most users need one or two things done very well. Open models let you specialize at the expense of generalization, which is the right tradeoff for most use cases.
concepts.importance: Provides the economic and practical rationale for why post-training specialization on open models can outperform frontier models — not because open models are inherently smarter, but because domain-specific optimization beats general-purpose capability for most real-world tasks.

concepts.name: Open vs. closed model coexistence
concepts.explanation: Closed models (OpenAI, Anthropic) serve as accessible consumer layers like Macs, while open models form the Linux layer running enterprises and clouds. Both gain usage and serve different segments — closed models are not the enemy.
concepts.importance: Provides a nuanced ecosystem model that avoids false binaries, helping practitioners understand where open and closed models each add value and how to architect systems that leverage both layers appropriately.

concepts.name: Open model capability trajectory
concepts.explanation: Vincent predicts open models will reach frontier-level (Fable-level) capability within 12 months, enabling a wave of new AI startups — similar to how Cursor only took off once Opus became good enough for coding.
concepts.importance: Sets a concrete timeline for when open models become viable for mainstream production use, which has major implications for startup strategy, investment decisions, and enterprise AI roadmap planning.

concepts.name: Knowledge worker agent shift
concepts.explanation: Predicted transition from chatbots and coding agents to general knowledge worker agents over the next 12 months. This represents a capability expansion from narrow task automation to broad knowledge work, driven by open model specialization and RL environments.
concepts.importance: Identifies the next major platform shift in AI applications — from task-specific assistants to general-purpose knowledge worker agents — which is what the open model stack is being built to enable.

concepts.name: Jevons paradox in AI economics
concepts.explanation: Per-token costs dropped significantly from GPT-4 to GPT-5.5, but total tokens per session rose exponentially, increasing total session costs despite lower unit prices. This makes cost predictability a structural challenge for closed-API consumers.
concepts.importance: Explains why declining per-token prices don't solve the enterprise cost problem — the economic dynamics of AI inference create a paradox where cheaper tokens drive more usage, not less spending. This strengthens the case for self-hosted open models with fixed compute costs.

concepts.name: Sovereign intelligence and capability restrictions
concepts.explanation: Lucas raises sovereign intelligence concerns about politicized capability restrictions, arguing that open models are essential for ensuring intelligence remains broadly accessible and not subject to geopolitical access controls.
concepts.importance: Connects the open model debate to national security and geopolitical considerations, elevating it from a technical choice to a strategic imperative for organizations and governments concerned about AI sovereignty.

concepts.name: Diffusion models for text generation
concepts.explanation: Chris predicts large architecture shifts toward diffusion-based text models, which are better suited to consumer hardware constraints than current autoregressive architectures.
concepts.importance: Points to a potential paradigm shift in text model architecture that could reshape the open model landscape, particularly for on-device deployment where compute and memory constraints favor diffusion-based generation.

concepts.name: Local model adoption trajectory
concepts.explanation: Lucas estimates perhaps 0.000001% of AI users have ever run an open model locally, and hopes this rises to 10–15% of AI users within the year, calling this the most consequential year for how AI gets distributed.
concepts.importance: Quantifies the current adoption gap for local AI and sets a concrete target, framing the distribution challenge as the key bottleneck for the open model ecosystem rather than raw model capability.

concepts.name: Post-training specialization pipeline
concepts.explanation: Using RL and fine-tuning to customize open models for domain-specific use cases, enabling specialized models that beat frontier models on specific tasks at lower cost. The Ramp case study demonstrates a company specializing an open model for finance automation in 1–2 weeks, beating Opus at a fraction of Haiku's cost.
concepts.importance: Central engineering practice advocated by the panel — post-training is the most accessible and economically viable customization layer for open models, bridging the gap between general-purpose weights and production-grade domain-specific agents.

concepts.name: Data flywheel through output ownership
concepts.explanation: Capturing production traces from open model deployments and using them for continual fine-tuning. Closed-API TOS prohibits training on outputs, while open models let users save all traces for fine-tuning or signal extraction, creating a self-reinforcing improvement loop.
concepts.importance: Fundamental architectural advantage of open models — the ability to own and reuse model outputs for continuous improvement is a structural capability gap that closed APIs cannot bridge, making it a key decision factor for enterprise AI deployment.

concepts.name: OpenMDW licensing model
concepts.explanation: A permissive license covering weights, data, software, and documentation as a unified whole, with an explicit Output clarity provision permitting training on model-generated outputs. Adopted by Arcee's Trinity family (May 2026) with NVIDIA announcing plans to adopt it for Nemotron.
concepts.importance: Closes a legal gap in the open model stack by making output-based training explicitly permissible, which is the legal foundation that enables the data flywheel concept. Without this, the economic case for open model specialization is weakened.

concepts.name: Model inspectability as trust mechanism
concepts.explanation: Open models are inspectable at the file and code level — they are directories of files with matrices that can be viewed and code that can be read. This enables trust through transparency, unlike closed APIs where internal claims are unverifiable by construction.
concepts.importance: Reframes trust as an engineering property (inspectability) rather than a policy assertion, which is foundational to the panel's argument that open models are more trustworthy, not less, than closed alternatives.

concepts.name: RL environments for domain-specific agents
concepts.explanation: Building domain-specific RL environments to train and deploy agents for specialized tasks at production scale. Prime Intellect's open-source Verifiers library and Prime-RL framework (verified first-party) implement this: creating environments, training agents, deploying to millions of users, and continuously learning from production traces.
concepts.importance: Represents the concrete engineering tooling that makes post-training specialization practical — the panel argues this is the path to deploying general knowledge worker agents and achieving continuous improvement from production data.

concepts.name: Model-harness co-design
concepts.explanation: The practice of blending the model and its application harness to create superior agentic experiences. OpenAI's Deep Research is cited as a paradigmatic example where RL on O3 with test-time compute outperformed simple search loops. The 'mismanaged genius' concept argues that fitting a model to a specific harness outperforms optimizing for all harnesses.
concepts.importance: Challenges the conventional approach of treating models as general-purpose APIs; argues that the most meaningful AI applications emerge from co-designing the model, harness, and product together, which is only possible with open weights.

concepts.name: On-device inference
concepts.explanation: Running capable models locally on phones and laptops, reducing API dependence for daily tasks. A 4-billion-parameter model already runs on phones and is more useful than GPT-4 was at launch. Chris predicts most daily AI tasks won't require an API within the year, with capable models running on MacBooks.
concepts.importance: Represents a platform-shift thesis where local compute enables next-generation AI applications, similar to how Cursor only took off once Opus became good enough for coding. This has major implications for inference architecture, edge deployment, and the future of consumer AI.

concepts.name: Agent operating systems
concepts.explanation: Predicted shift from traditional operating systems to systems that orchestrate AI agents for user tasks. Computers will ship with agent operating systems instead of traditional OSs.
concepts.importance: Represents a foundational platform shift that would reshape the entire computing stack — from OS design to application architecture to the role of APIs — positioning AI agents as the primary interaction layer for computing.

concepts.name: Cost predictability via open model deployment
concepts.explanation: Open models let organizations control costs without vendor dependencies on pricing changes or model deprecations. Despite per-token costs dropping from GPT-4 to GPT-5.5, total session costs rise because token counts per session grow exponentially — a Jevons paradox effect that makes cost predictability a CFO trust issue.
concepts.importance: Addresses a core enterprise adoption barrier: predictable costs are essential for AI budgeting, and open models provide cost sovereignty that closed APIs structurally cannot, since vendors can change pricing or deprecate models at will.

concepts.name: Open-source community optimization (Linux analogy)
concepts.explanation: Drawing on the Linux analogy, hyper-optimization requires a broad community of contributors working under resource constraints. Linux runs the internet precisely because it was hyper-optimized by a community, something closed companies cannot replicate by shutting people out of the room.
concepts.importance: Provides a proven historical precedent for why open-source infrastructure eventually displaces closed alternatives in enterprise and cloud, grounding the panel's strategic argument in a well-understood engineering and economic pattern.

sections.title: Welcome and panel introductions
sections.summary: Carter Abdallah introduces the panel on local, sovereign AI models. Vincent Weisser (Prime Intellect) describes ensuring open frontier intelligence across the full training stack. Lucas Atkins (Arcee AI) explains pivoting to pretrain a 400B-parameter model in six months after the West lost open-model leadership. Chris Alexiuk (NVIDIA Nemotron) outlines a philosophy of full openness—weights, data, methodology, frameworks—and the mantra that faster models are smarter models.

sections.title: Is open source actually less trustworthy
sections.summary: Carter raises the counter-narrative that open source is chaotic and less trustworthy. Lucas argues trust is conflated with safety but is distinct: open models are inspectable directories of files with readable code, whereas closed API claims are unverifiable. He cites Anthropic pulling back Fable access as the moment enterprises adopted Chinese open models for guaranteed availability rather than benchmark superiority.

sections.title: Releasing the data sets alongside the weights
sections.summary: Chris explains that NVIDIA releases datasets and training environments alongside Nemotron weights so users can see what data shapes look like without reverse-engineering. Lucas notes datasets are visible on Hugging Face for Prime Intellect, Arcee, and NVIDIA, helping users inform their priors about model behavior.

sections.title: The open superintelligence stack and post-training as the accessible layer
sections.summary: Vincent describes Prime Intellect's work building RL and post-training infrastructure to enable enterprises to specialize open models like Trinity and Nemotron for specific use cases. He cites companies like Ramp or Saber automating finance in one to two weeks with better performance than Opus at a fraction of Haiku's cost. The key value proposition is creating specialized models that beat frontier models while being faster and cheaper.

sections.title: Making your costs predictable
sections.summary: Carter frames cost predictability as a trust issue for CFOs. Enterprises have massive token spends and are cutting back on Opus usage. Despite per-token costs dropping from GPT-4 to GPT-5.5, total session costs rise because token counts per session grow exponentially. Open models let organizations control costs without vendor dependencies on pricing changes or model deprecations.

sections.title: When the model and the harness blend together
sections.summary: Carter argues the most meaningful AI applications blend harness, model, and product, citing OpenAI's Deep Research as a paradigmatic example where RL on O3 with test-time compute created a superior agentic experience. Chris introduces the 'mismanaged genius' concept: a model tuned across every harness is optimal for nobody's. Open weights let builders post-train models for their specific harness, achieving customization impossible with closed models.

sections.title: Owning your outputs and the open MDW license
sections.summary: Carter explains that closed-model providers monetize user data and use TOS to prevent training on outputs. Open models let users save all traces for fine-tuning or signal extraction, enabling a data flywheel. Lucas highlights that Nemotron and Trinity adopted the open MDW license, which explicitly permits using outputs to train models—unlike restrictive closed-API terms. Vincent and Lucas issue a call to action: take the best open model and post-train on your harness to build AI-native products.

sections.title: Post-training unlocks new use cases
sections.summary: Carter frames optimization as the third topic: with the right customization, open models can exceed frontier model performance on specific use cases. Vincent describes building RL environments for specific domains, deploying agents to production users (e.g., a million accountants), and continuously learning from production traces. He cites computer use agents as a major growth area where millions of production traces enable continuous improvement. The broader open ecosystem drives down inference and training costs.

sections.title: You do not need frontier intelligence for most tasks
sections.summary: Chris argues that most people do not need frontier-level intelligence for 90% of tasks. Most users need one or two things done very well. Open models let you specialize at the expense of generalization. He draws the Linux analogy: hyper-optimization requires a broad community of contributors working under resource constraints, something closed companies cannot replicate by shutting people out of the room.

sections.title: Closed models are not the enemy
sections.summary: Lucas clarifies that closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic are beneficial and he uses them daily. He frames open models as the Linux layer running enterprises and clouds, while closed APIs are like Macs—accessible and easy for consumers. The ecosystem will coexist: closed and open models both gain usage and serve different segments.

sections.title: Predictions for the next year
sections.summary: Vincent predicts open models will reach Fable-level capability within 12 months, enabling a wave of new AI startups—similar to how Cursor only took off once Opus became good enough for coding. He sees a shift from chatbots and coding agents to general knowledge worker agents. Lucas predicts this is the most consequential year for AI distribution, raises sovereign intelligence concerns about politicized capability restrictions, and hopes 10–15% of AI users will have run a model locally—up from a near-zero baseline. He calls on the community to advocate for open models against weaponized terms framing them as unsafe.

sections.title: Running everything on your laptop
sections.summary: Chris predicts most daily AI tasks won't require an API within the year, with capable models running locally on MacBooks. He expects swarms of specialized models to become important, large architecture shifts toward diffusion models for text better suited to consumer hardware, and computers shipping with agent operating systems instead of traditional OSs. Carter predicts the next iPhone's Siri will trigger mainstream AI engagement. Vincent sees a platform shift where on-device compute enables next-generation AI applications, and Chris notes a 4-billion-parameter model already runs on phones and is more useful than GPT-4 was at launch.

sections.title: Closing
sections.summary: Carter summarizes the inflection point: open source is entering public consciousness but few have had their aha moment yet, and this year has potential to change that. Lucas and Carter close with a call to action: builders in the room are essential to advocating for open models and ensuring intelligence remains broadly accessible, and without them the fight for open intelligence is lost.

organization.name: Prime Intellect
organization.summary: Prime Intellect, Inc. is a San Francisco-based AI infrastructure company operating as both a full-stack platform and an open research lab. Vincent Weisser is CEO & Co-Founder and Johannes Hagemann is CTO & Co-Founder. The company provides an integrated compute, training, inference, and sandbox stack branded as 'The Open Superintelligence Stack,' enabling organizations to train, deploy, and continuously improve their own models. The platform includes RL environments (built on the open-source Verifiers library with 2,500+ community environments), hosted training (Prime-RL framework), dedicated and serverless inference with LoRA support, and a global compute marketplace. Prime Intellect is backed by Founders Fund, NVIDIA, Intel, Andrej Karpathy, John Schulman, Dylan Patel, and Clem Delangue. Confirmed customers include Ramp (finance automation RL subagent) and Zapier (agent improvement loop). Prime Intellect is listed as a Nemotron Coalition partner on NVIDIA's official page.

technologies.label: NVIDIA Nemotron Open Model Family
technologies.summary: NVIDIA Nemotron is a family of open AI models characterized by full openness across weights, training data, methodology, and frameworks. The panel features Nemotron as the deployment and optimization layer of the open AI stack, with the 'faster models are smarter models' philosophy. Chris Alexiuk (NVIDIA) presents Nemotron's open philosophy — inspectable directories of files with readable code — as the trust mechanism distinguishing open models from unverifiable closed APIs. NVIDIA publishes weights and data on Hugging Face, lists Prime Intellect as a Nemotron Coalition partner, and announced plans to adopt OpenMDW-1.1. The panel cites a 4B-parameter Nemotron-class model already running on phones that is more useful than GPT-4 was at launch, and predicts capable local models on MacBooks within the year.
technologies.role: Chris Alexiuk represents NVIDIA Nemotron as one of three featured panelists, discussing the open model philosophy, the 'mismanaged genius' concept, the Linux analogy for open optimization, and predictions about local deployment, diffusion-based text architectures, and agent operating systems.

technologies.label: Arcee Trinity Open Model Family
technologies.summary: Arcee AI's Trinity is an open-weight model family including Trinity Large Thinking, Trinity Mini, and Trinity Nano. Arcee pretrained a 400-billion-parameter MoE model from scratch in six months after observing the West losing open-model leadership to China. The entire Trinity family moved to OpenMDW-1.1 on May 29, 2026, making output-based training explicitly permissible. Lucas Atkins (Arcee CTO) discusses trust as distinct from safety, argues open models are inspectable at the file and code level, and cites Anthropic pulling back Fable access as the moment enterprises adopted Chinese open models for guaranteed availability rather than benchmark superiority.
technologies.role: Lucas Atkins represents Arcee AI as one of three featured panelists, discussing the 400B model pretraining, the trust vs. safety distinction, model inspectability, the OpenMDW license adoption by Trinity and Nemotron, output ownership, and predictions about local model adoption and sovereign intelligence.

technologies.label: Prime Intellect Open Training Infrastructure
technologies.summary: Prime Intellect provides open training infrastructure including RL environments, hosted training, inference, and compute for open model post-training. The company maintains two verified first-party open-source repositories: Verifiers (a library for creating RL environments and evaluating LLMs, 4,530+ GitHub stars, integrated with an Environments Hub of 2,500+ community environments) and Prime-RL (an asynchronous RL framework scaling to 1,000+ GPUs). The verified Ramp case study confirms a specialized RL-trained subagent (Fast Ask) beat frontier models on spreadsheet search accuracy at faster speeds and a fraction of the cost. Vincent Weisser (CEO) describes building RL environments for domain-specific use cases, deploying agents to millions of users (e.g., accountants), and continuously improving from production traces including computer use agents.
technologies.role: Vincent Weisser represents Prime Intellect as one of three featured panelists, describing the company's role in building RL and post-training infrastructure, the Ramp/Saber finance automation case study, building RL environments for domain-specific agents, continuous learning from production traces, and predictions about open model capability trajectory and knowledge worker agents.

technologies.label: OpenMDW License
technologies.summary: OpenMDW (Open Model-Data-Weights) is a permissive AI model license stewarded by the Linux Foundation that covers weights, software, documentation, training data, and other artifacts as a unified whole. Version 1.1 includes an explicit Output clarity provision that addresses model-generated outputs, making it explicitly permissible to use model outputs for training. Arcee's Trinity family moved to OpenMDW-1.1 on May 29, 2026, and NVIDIA announced plans to adopt it across Nemotron and other model families. The panel identifies this license as the legal foundation enabling the data flywheel concept — closed-API terms of service prohibit training on outputs, while OpenMDW explicitly permits it, creating a structural advantage for open models in building self-improving agent systems.
technologies.role: Discussed as a key enabler of data flywheels and output ownership. Lucas Atkins confirms Nemotron and Trinity adopted the OpenMDW license, and Carter Abdallah frames it as the legal mechanism that distinguishes open models from closed APIs whose TOS prevent training on outputs. Vincent Weisser and Lucas issue a call to action: take the best open model with OpenMDW licensing and post-train on your harness to build AI-native products.
